decks.domain: Marking, signal and warning-sign look-alikes, plus continuation facts moved from part C

cards.front: What kinds of information do pavement lines and symbols give drivers?
cards.back: Pavement lines and symbols tell drivers where lanes split, where passing or changing lanes is allowed, which lanes are for turning, where walkers cross, and where to stop.

cards.front: Which kind of pavement line may be crossed to pass, and which should not be?
cards.back: A broken line may be crossed to pass, while a solid line should not be crossed to pass.

cards.front: What do yellow lines divide, and what do white lines divide?
cards.back: Yellow lines divide traffic going in opposite directions, and white lines divide traffic going the same direction.

cards.front: What does a yellow line on your left tell you, compared with a white line on your left, and what does a solid white line often mark?
cards.back: A yellow line on your left means traffic beyond it is coming toward you, while a white line on your left means it is going your way; a solid white line often marks the right edge of the road.

cards.front: How is the center of a four-lane road marked, and may you cross it to pass?
cards.back: On a four-lane road the center is marked with two solid yellow lines, and you must never cross them to pass.

cards.front: How is a no passing zone on a two-lane road marked, where is it placed, and when should your pass be finished?
cards.back: A no passing zone on a two-lane road is marked by a solid yellow line and is placed on hills or curves where you cannot see far enough ahead, so finish any pass before reaching it.

cards.front: When must you not pass with respect to a solid yellow line, and what must you see before passing on any two-lane road?
cards.back: Do not pass when a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, and on any two-lane road never pass without seeing enough clear road, even if there is no marking.

cards.front: Why should you not pass using the shoulder?
cards.back: Do not pass using the shoulder, because drivers do not expect a car there and may pull onto it without checking.

decks.domain: Missouri pavement markings, traffic officers, traffic signals, sign shapes and colors, and warning signs

cards.front: When a sign or signal requires a stop, where do you stop?
cards.back: When a sign or signal requires a stop, stop before the stop line, or before the crosswalk if one is marked.

cards.front: What do crosswalks mark on the road?
cards.back: Crosswalks mark the area where pedestrians are meant to cross the road.

cards.front: Which pedestrians must you yield to at crosswalks, and why stay alert at intersections with no painted crosswalk?
cards.back: Yield to pedestrians who are in a crosswalk or about to step into one, and stay alert at intersections without marked crosswalks, because not every crosswalk is painted.

cards.front: In a dual-use lane with turn and straight arrows, when may you turn and when must you wait?
cards.back: In a dual-use lane with turn and straight arrows, you may turn or go straight when both arrows show on the signal, but if only the straight arrow is lit you must wait for the turn arrow before turning.

cards.front: How is a shared center lane bordered, who uses it and for what, and when do you leave it?
cards.back: A shared center lane, bordered by a solid yellow and a dashed yellow line on each side, is used by traffic from both directions for left turns, or U-turns where allowed, and you turn out of it as soon as your path is clear.

cards.front: How are marked left-turn lanes painted on the pavement?
cards.back: Marked left-turn lanes use solid yellow lines together with thick yellow stripes on the pavement.

cards.front: What should you do instead of backing up after missing a turn or exit?
cards.back: Never back up in a travel lane; if you miss a turn or exit, keep going to a place where you can safely turn around.

cards.front: May you stop in a travel lane when lost, broken down or dropping someone off, and what should you do?
cards.back: Never stop in a travel lane, whether you are lost, broken down or dropping someone off; keep going until you can safely pull off.

cards.front: With three or more lanes going your way, which lane should you use, and when is the center lane better?
cards.back: With three or more lanes going your way, stay in the right lane except to pass, but use the center lane if a lot of traffic is entering the right lane.

cards.front: Which lane on a multi-lane road is meant for passing, and why is passing on the right risky?
cards.back: On multi-lane roads the left-most lane is meant for passing, and passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you and may move over.

decks.domain: Marking, signal and warning-sign look-alikes, plus continuation facts moved from part C

cards.front: What does traffic control cover, and who besides signals and signs can direct traffic?
cards.back: Traffic control covers signals, signs and pavement markings, and it can also come from police, highway workers or school crossing guards, whose directions you must follow.

cards.front: If a traffic officer signals you to stop at a green light, what do you do?
cards.back: Always obey a traffic officer over any sign or signal, so if an officer signals you to stop at a green light, you stop.

cards.front: What does a flashing red light mean, and what does a flashing yellow light mean?
cards.back: A flashing red light has the same meaning as a stop sign, and a flashing yellow light means slow down and go ahead with caution.

cards.front: At a steady red light, where do you stop and how long do you wait?
cards.back: At a steady red light, stop at the stop line, the crosswalk or before the intersection and wait for green unless you are turning right.

cards.front: When may you turn right on a red light?
cards.back: After a complete stop you may turn right on red if no pedestrians or traffic are in the way, unless a No Right Turn On Red sign is posted.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow light warn, and when should you still go through?
cards.back: A steady yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red, so stop unless you are already in the intersection or too close to stop safely.

cards.front: What does a green light let you do, and whom must you yield to first?
cards.back: A green light lets you go through, but first yield to vehicles and pedestrians still in the intersection.

cards.front: How does a flashing red signal differ from a steady red?
cards.back: A flashing red signal works like a stop sign, while a steady red means stop and wait for green except for a permitted right turn.

cards.front: How does a flashing yellow light differ from a steady yellow?
cards.back: A flashing yellow light means slow and proceed with caution, while a steady yellow means the light is about to turn red and you should stop if you safely can.

cards.front: When may traffic signals flash in all directions?
cards.back: Signals may flash in all directions during emergencies, at night, in periods of light traffic and at special events.

cards.front: How do you treat a traffic signal that is dark or not working?
cards.back: A traffic signal that is dark or not working is treated as a four-way stop.

decks.domain: Missouri pavement markings, traffic officers, traffic signals, sign shapes and colors, and warning signs

cards.front: What do you get in a permissive left-turn phase, and what must you wait for?
cards.back: In a permissive left-turn phase you get a circular green or a flashing yellow arrow and must wait for a big enough gap in oncoming traffic.

cards.front: When do you turn in a protected left-turn phase, and what holds oncoming traffic?
cards.back: In a protected left-turn phase you turn only on a green arrow while oncoming traffic is held by a red light.

cards.front: What does a protected and permissive phase alternate between, and when must you pick a gap yourself?
cards.back: A protected and permissive phase alternates between a green arrow and a circular green or flashing yellow arrow, when you must pick a gap yourself.

cards.front: What does a steady red arrow mean, and whom may you still need to yield to?
cards.back: A steady red arrow means stop and wait for green or a flashing yellow arrow, and you may still need to yield to pedestrians.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow arrow follow, what can it change to, and how should you respond?
cards.back: A steady yellow arrow follows a green arrow and warns it will change to a circular green, a flashing yellow arrow or red, so be ready to yield or stop.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow arrow let you do, and on what conditions?
cards.back: A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn in the arrow's direction, but only after a safe gap in oncoming traffic opens and while yielding to pedestrians.

cards.front: What does a green arrow let you do, and what conditions must hold?
cards.back: A green arrow lets you go the way it points, provided you are in the proper lane and no traffic or pedestrians are in your path.

cards.front: How does a green arrow differ from a flashing yellow arrow?
cards.back: A green arrow gives a clear path in its direction, while a flashing yellow arrow allows the turn only after you find a gap and yield.

cards.front: How does a steady red arrow differ from a steady yellow arrow?
cards.back: A steady red arrow means wait, but a steady yellow arrow means the green arrow is ending and you should get ready to yield or stop.

decks.domain: Missouri pavement markings, traffic officers, traffic signals, sign shapes and colors, and warning signs

cards.front: What do the octagon, triangle, pentagon, pennant and diamond sign shapes mean?
cards.back: Sign shapes carry meaning: an octagon is stop, a triangle is yield, a pentagon is school, a pennant is a no passing zone and a diamond is a warning.

cards.front: What do a vertical rectangle, a horizontal rectangle and a round sign or crossbuck mean?
cards.back: A vertical rectangle is a regulatory sign, a horizontal rectangle is a guide sign, and a round sign or crossbuck means railroad.

cards.front: What do red, white and black, yellow, and yellow green mean on signs?
cards.back: Sign colors carry meaning too: red is for stop, yield or prohibited, white and black for regulatory, yellow for warning and yellow green for school.

cards.front: What do orange, green, blue and brown mean on signs?
cards.back: Orange signs are for construction, green for direction and distance, blue for motorist services, and brown for public recreation and cultural interests.

cards.front: Which colors are regulatory, and how is yellow green used differently from yellow?
cards.back: Both white and black are listed as regulatory sign colors, while yellow green is reserved for school signs and yellow for general warnings.

cards.front: Which shape marks a no passing zone, and which marks a school sign?
cards.back: A pennant shape marks a no passing zone, while a pentagon marks a school sign.

cards.front: What do many regulatory signs look like, and what topics do they cover?
cards.back: Many regulatory signs are white squares or rectangles with black or red letters or symbols covering direction, lane use, turns, speed and parking.

cards.front: What does a red circle with a red slash over a symbol mean?
cards.back: A red circle with a red slash over a symbol means that action is not allowed, such as no left turn or no U-turn.

cards.front: Besides no left turn, no right turn and no U-turn, what are two more prohibition sign examples?
cards.back: No Trucks and No Bicycles are examples of prohibition signs alongside No Left Turn, No Right Turn and No U-Turn.

decks.domain: Missouri pavement markings, traffic officers, traffic signals, sign shapes and colors, and warning signs

cards.front: What do warning signs usually look like, and what do they tell you to do?
cards.back: Warning signs are usually yellow diamonds with black letters or symbols and tell you to slow down and be ready to stop for a hazard or special situation ahead.

cards.front: What do the Stop Ahead and Signal Ahead signs warn of, and how should you prepare?
cards.back: A Stop Ahead sign means a stop sign is coming on your road, and a Signal Ahead sign means a traffic light is coming; be ready to stop for either.

cards.front: What should you do at a School Crossing sign and at a Pedestrian Crossing sign?
cards.back: At a School Crossing sign, slow down and watch for children crossing, and at a Pedestrian Crossing sign, slow down and yield to people in the crosswalk.

cards.front: What color change is coming for the School Crossing sign?
cards.back: The School Crossing sign is being changed to a yellow green color over a transition the guide says will take effect within ten years.

cards.front: What does an Added Lane sign mean, and how does a Merge sign differ?
cards.back: An Added Lane sign means traffic from another road gets its own new lane, so no merge is needed, while a Merge sign means entering vehicles may move into your lane.

cards.front: What does a Lane Ends Merge Left sign mean for a driver in the right lane?
cards.back: A Lane Ends Merge Left sign means two lanes become one, and a driver in the right lane must merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane.

cards.front: What do the Added Lane and Merge signs share, and what separates them?
cards.back: The Added Lane and Merge signs both warn of traffic entering from another road; the difference is whether the entering traffic gets its own lane or moves into yours.

cards.front: What does a T Intersection Ahead sign mean for your road?
cards.back: A T Intersection Ahead sign means your road ends and you must turn right or left.

cards.front: What does an Intersection sign warn of, and how does a Side Road Ahead sign differ?
cards.back: An Intersection sign warns that another road crosses yours, and a Side Road Ahead sign warns that a road joins from the side the sign shows.

cards.front: What does a Roundabout Ahead sign tell you to do?
cards.back: A Roundabout Ahead sign tells you to slow to the posted speed restriction and use the roundabout rules.

cards.front: What does a Side Road Railroad Crossing sign warn of?
cards.back: A Side Road Railroad Crossing sign warns that tracks cross just beside an intersection, so take care crossing them.

decks.domain: Missouri pavement markings, traffic officers, traffic signals, sign shapes and colors, and warning signs

cards.front: What does a reverse turn sign warn of, and what top speed does it recommend?
cards.back: A reverse turn sign warns of two turns in opposite directions, the second possibly sharper, with a recommended top speed of thirty miles per hour or less.

cards.front: How does a turn sign's recommended speed compare with a curve sign's?
cards.back: A turn sign marks a sharp turn with a recommended maximum of thirty miles per hour or less, while a curve sign marks a curve whose recommended speed is below the posted highway limit.

cards.front: Which signs share a top recommended speed of thirty miles per hour or less, and what does a curve sign say instead?
cards.back: Turn signs and reverse turn signs both point to a top recommended speed of thirty miles per hour or less, while a curve sign only says the advised speed is below the highway's posted limit.

cards.front: What does an advisory speed plate give, and how should you treat it in rain, snow or ice?
cards.back: An advisory speed plate on a curve or turn sign gives the recommended speed, and you should never go faster than it in rain, snow or ice even if it feels safe in good weather.

cards.front: What does an Exit Speed Advisory sign show?
cards.back: An Exit Speed Advisory sign shows the recommended speed for a highway exit ramp.

cards.front: What do a large arrow on the outside of a turn and chevron signs at curves stress?
cards.back: A large arrow placed on the outside of a turn and chevron signs at curves both stress the need to slow down for a sharp change of direction.

cards.front: What does a reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle mean?
cards.back: A reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle means it travels under twenty-five miles per hour, as farm vehicles and construction equipment often do.

cards.front: What does a Slippery When Wet sign warn of, and what does a Soft Shoulder sign mean?
cards.back: A Slippery When Wet sign warns of a road that gets unusually slick in wet weather, and a Soft Shoulder sign means do not drive off the pavement.

cards.front: What do the Begin Divided Roadway and End Divided Roadway signs warn of?
cards.back: A Begin Divided Roadway sign warns that a median or barrier will soon split the two directions of traffic, and End Divided Roadway warns that the split is ending.

cards.front: What do object markers warn of, and what do they remind you not to do?
cards.back: Object markers warn of something in the road or right at its edge, a reminder not to drift out of your lane.

cards.front: What does a Bicycle Share the Road sign warn of?
cards.back: A Bicycle Share the Road sign warns that cyclists may be riding in the same lane as motor traffic.

recap_hooks.text: Pavement lines show where passing is allowed: broken lines let you pass and solid lines say do not, while yellow splits opposite traffic and white splits traffic going your way.
A four-lane road's double solid yellow center is never crossed to pass, and a no passing zone sits on hills or curves, so finish passing before it.
The shoulder is not a passing lane, because drivers may pull onto it without checking.
Stop before the stop line or a marked crosswalk, and yield to people crossing or about to step out, even where no crosswalk is painted.
With only the straight arrow lit, wait for the turn arrow; the shared center lane serves both directions, while marked left-turn lanes have thick yellow stripes.
Never back up or stop in a travel lane, keep right except to pass, and remember the left-most lane is for passing.
An officer's directions come before any sign or signal, and police, highway workers and crossing guards all direct traffic.
Steady red means wait for green unless turning right after a full stop, steady yellow means red is coming, and green still means yield first.
Flashing red works like a stop sign, flashing yellow means go ahead with caution, and a dark signal is a four-way stop.
Permissive means wait for a gap, protected means a green arrow while oncoming traffic sits at red, and the combined phase switches between them.
A green arrow gives a clear path, while a flashing yellow arrow lets you turn only after a safe gap and yielding.
A steady red arrow means wait, and a steady yellow arrow means the green arrow is ending.
Octagon stop, triangle yield, pentagon school, pennant no passing, diamond warning; tall rectangles regulate and wide ones guide.
Red stops or forbids, yellow warns, yellow green marks schools, orange is construction, green directs, blue serves and brown is recreation.
Regulatory signs are often white with black or red, and a red circle and slash means that action is not allowed.
Yellow diamonds warn you to slow and be ready to stop, whether a stop sign, a signal, a school crossing or a pedestrian crossing lies ahead.
Added Lane gives entering traffic its own lane, Merge sends it into yours, and Lane Ends Merge Left means the right lane merges and yields.
A T intersection ends your road, a side road joins from one side, a roundabout means slow down and follow its rules, and a side road railroad crossing puts tracks beside the intersection.
Turn and reverse turn signs point to thirty miles per hour or less, a curve sign only says slower than the posted limit, and arrows and chevrons say slow for the bend.
Never beat the advisory plate in rain, snow or ice, use the exit advisory speed on ramps, and watch for divided roadways and cyclists sharing the lane.
An orange triangle marks a vehicle under twenty-five miles per hour, wet roads can turn slick, a soft shoulder means stay on the pavement, and object markers flag hazards at the edge.
